body.heading: Four acts, one animal
paragraphs: A butterfly’s life runs in four acts: egg, larva, pupa and adult. The larva — the caterpillar — has one overwhelming job: eat and grow. It sheds its skin several times as it outgrows it.
When it is ready, it forms a pupa, called a chrysalis in butterflies. From the outside, almost nothing seems to happen for days or weeks. Inside, it is the busiest time of the animal’s life.

body.heading: The great rebuild
paragraphs: Within the chrysalis, much of the caterpillar’s body breaks down into a kind of living soup. But not everything dissolves. Small clusters of cells, called imaginal discs, survive — and each one grows into a part of the adult: a wing, a leg, an antenna.

Remarkably, experiments suggest that some learning can survive the rebuild: moths trained as caterpillars to avoid a smell have been shown to avoid it as adults. A memory, carried through a near-total reconstruction.

body.heading: Why live two lives?
paragraphs: The two stages barely resemble each other, and that is the point. Caterpillars are eating machines specialised for growth; butterflies are flying machines specialised for mating and spreading eggs across many plants.
Because the stages eat different foods, parents and offspring never compete for the same meal. Two lives, one animal, no rivalry.

takeaway: Metamorphosis lets one animal live two different lives — an eating machine first, then a flying one — rebuilt from small clusters of patient cells.
